title: Concerto for Two Violins in D minor
hook: Two violins as equal partners, chasing and answering each other, with one of Bach’s best-loved slow movements at the centre.

painting.title: The Sense of Hearing
painting.collection: Yale Center for British Art, New Haven
painting.pairingNote: Music at home in the 1740s by a Berlin-born painter, a violin with harpsichord and cello beneath it, the same partnership of strings and continuo that carries Bach’s concerto.

facts: Bach wrote this concerto in Leipzig, probably in 1730 or early 1731, for the Collegium Musicum, a society of students and professional musicians that he directed from 1729. They gave free concerts at Gottfried Zimmermann’s coffee house, where the audience paid only for its coffee. Bach’s own handwritten parts for the two soloists survive from those years.

There are two solo violins, a small string band and the [[continuo|continuo]] of harpsichord and bass instruments. The two soloists are not rivals. They are equal partners: one plays a phrase, the other answers or takes it over, and often they play the same tune a moment apart.

Bach learned the Italian concerto by studying Vivaldi, and the outer movements follow its plan: a refrain for the band, the [[ritornello|ritornello]], comes back in different keys between the soloists’ passages. But Bach fills it with [[counterpoint|counterpoint]], independent lines woven together.

A few years later he arranged the whole concerto for two harpsichords, a tone lower in C minor (BWV 1062). Today the violin version is by far the better known, above all for its singing slow movement.
bigPicture.inOneLine: a busy, serious dialogue (I), a long duet of two singing voices (II), a fierce chase (III).

movements.heading: Vivace
movements.summary: The movement opens like a [[fugue|fugue]]: one group of violins in the band starts a busy tune, a second group enters with it a little higher, and the texture fills out. When the two soloists arrive they bring a new, livelier idea, which one plays and the other immediately repeats. The band’s fugue tune and the soloists’ dialogue take turns to the end.

mainIdeas.name: The fugue tune
mainIdeas.description: a determined line of quick notes, passed from part to part in the band.

mainIdeas.name: The soloists’ theme
mainIdeas.description: a leaping, bright figure that one violin plays and the other echoes, a step higher or lower.

stops.hear: A busy tune starts in one group of violins; another group answers it higher up, and the sound fills out
The two solo violins step forward with a new, leaping idea; one plays it, the other copies it straight away
The fugue tune again, in the band, in a different key
The soloists trade phrases faster, the lines overlapping
The opening tune is back in D minor, in the whole band

notice: When the soloists enter, try to hear which violin leads and which follows. A moment later they will swap roles.

movements.heading: Largo ma non tanto
movements.summary: A slow, swaying movement in F major, in the lilting rhythm of a [[siciliano|siciliano]]. The band plays soft, steady chords underneath, and above them the two soloists sing one long duet: one starts a melody, the other enters with the same melody a few bars later, and their lines wind around each other, crossing and parting.

mainIdeas.name: The duet melody
mainIdeas.description: a long, singing line, first in one violin, then in the other.

mainIdeas.name: The accompaniment
mainIdeas.description: quiet, gently pulsing chords in the band, never pushing.

stops.hear: Soft, rocking chords in the band; one solo violin begins a long, singing melody
stops.happening: The duet begins in F major

stops.hear: The second violin enters with the same melody while the first continues above or below it
The music darkens into minor keys; the two lines press closer together and grow more intense
stops.happening: The emotional peak of the movement

stops.label: Near the end
stops.hear: The two violins come to rest together, softly, back in F major

notice: Follow one violin for a whole minute, then switch to the other. Neither is the accompaniment; each has the melody in turn.

notes.title: In this recording
notes.body: The English Concert play on period instruments, and Trevor Pinnock directs from the harpsichord. Their Largo lasts six and a half minutes and keeps moving; the Oistrakhs’ recording (also recommended) takes about a minute longer.

movements.heading: Allegro
movements.summary: A fast, driving finale in D minor. It opens with the two soloists in a close [[canon|canon]]: the second violin plays the same tune as the first, only one beat behind, so the two seem to be chasing each other. The band answers with hard, forceful chords, and the chase goes on through several keys before the opening returns.

mainIdeas.name: The chase
mainIdeas.description: the soloists’ tune, played by both violins one beat apart.

mainIdeas.name: The band’s answer
mainIdeas.description: short, strong chords and rushing figures, almost stormy.

stops.hear: The two solo violins start almost together, the second a beat behind the first; the band drives underneath
The full band takes over, loud and insistent
The soloists again, with quick runs and broken chords tossed between them
stops.happening: A solo episode, moving to new keys

stops.hear: The chase returns in another key
stops.happening: The canon, now away from home

stops.hear: The soloists’ figures grow more urgent; the band joins with heavy chords

stops.label: Last 20 seconds
stops.hear: The opening canon in D minor, then a short, firm close

notice: At the start, listen for the echo: the second violin is exactly one beat behind the first. It is the same principle as a round, only very fast.

threads.title: Two equals
threads.body: In all three movements the two violins share the material. Bach gives neither the leading part for long.

threads.title: Imitation everywhere
threads.body: A fugue in the band (I), a canon in the duet (II), a close canon in the chase (III): the concerto is built from voices copying each other.

threads.title: A concert in a coffee house
threads.body: The concerto was written for public concerts by students and professionals in Leipzig, not for the church. In the 20th century George Balanchine made a ballet of it, *Concerto Barocco*, in which two ballerinas follow the two violins.
